goldens.comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/GroupPermissionsV2.java:70 — The all-groups `view` scope satisfies `canManage()`, so a caller granted read-only group access can create or re-parent groups through endpoints guarded by `requireManage()`.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at GroupPermissionsV2.java lines 65-72, the canManage() method returns true if hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE) - meaning VIEW scope satisfies canManage(). This is inconsistent with the documented behavior in GroupPermissionEvaluator.java which states canManage() should require MANAGE permission. The canManage(GroupModel group) method at lines 74-80 correctly only checks for MANAGE scope, but the no-arg canManage() incorrectly includes VIEW. This would allow users with only VIEW permission on all-groups to pass requireManage() checks, enabling them to create groups or perform other management operations.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/GroupPermissionsV2.java:122 — Group authorization-resource IDs are passed as group names and returned as model group IDs, so `view-members`/`manage-members` grants do not expose the authorized users in list and count APIs.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in GroupPermissionsV2.java:122, the method `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` iterates over resources of type GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE and checks permissions using `groupResource.getId()`. The finding claims there's a mismatch between group names and IDs, but examining the code: `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, groupResource -> { if (hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...)) { granted.add(groupResource.getId()); } })` - this adds the resource ID to the granted set. Looking at AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup(), it returns `group.getId()` (the group ID), and resources are created with the group ID as the name. The finding's claim about IDs being passed as names and returned incorrectly is not substantiated by the diff - the code consistently uses group IDs throughout.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/GroupPermissionsV2.java:70 — A realm-wide VIEW grant makes canManage() true, allowing group creation despite lacking MANAGE scope.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at GroupPermissionsV2.java lines 65-72, the canManage() method returns true if hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE) returns true. This means having VIEW permission on groups would make canManage() return true, which is incorrect - VIEW should not grant MANAGE capabilities. The method should only check for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This is inconsistent with canManage(GroupModel group) at line 79 which correctly only checks for MANAGE scope.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/GroupPermissionsV2.java:122 — The code treats authorization resource IDs as group IDs/names, so per-group member-view grants cannot produce a usable group filter.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at GroupPermissionsV2.java:122, the code iterates over resources of type GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE and adds `groupResource.getId()` to the granted set. However, examining the AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource() method, when creating a group resource, it calls `resolveGroup()` which returns `group.getId()` as the name. The resource is created with `id` as the resource name (line 119-120 in AdminPermissionsSchema). So `groupResource.getId()` returns the authorization resource's internal ID, not the group's ID. The method should be using `groupResource.getName()` to get the actual group ID that was stored as the resource name. This would cause the returned set to contain wrong IDs, breaking the group filtering functionality.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/GroupPermissionsV2.java:122 — Authorization resource IDs are passed through an API expecting group IDs and then returned as group IDs, coupling two unrelated identifier domains and breaking member filtering.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at GroupPermissionsV2.java:122, the code iterates over resources of type GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE and adds `groupResource.getId()` to the granted set. However, `groupResource.getId()` returns the Resource's ID (authorization resource ID), not the group's ID. In contrast, the V1 implementation in GroupPermissions.java extracts the group ID from the resource name using `resource.getName().substring(RESOURCE_NAME_PREFIX.length())`. The V2 code incorrectly returns authorization resource IDs instead of actual group IDs, which would break the member filtering functionality that expects group IDs.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/GroupPermissionsV2.java:168 — Extending the legacy GroupPermissions implementation forces V2 to expose eight management methods that only fail at runtime, so evaluator and management concerns should be separated at the type boundary.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that GroupPermissionsV2 extends GroupPermissions and overrides 8 methods (isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, viewMembersPermission, manageMembersPermission, manageMembershipPermission, viewPermission, managePermission, resource, getPermissions) to throw UnsupportedOperationException at runtime (lines 168-211). This is a valid architectural concern - the V2 class inherits the GroupPermissionManagement interface through GroupPermissions but cannot properly implement those methods, leading to runtime failures instead of compile-time type safety. However, this is a design/architecture issue rather than a bug since the code functions as intended for the V2 permission evaluation use case.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/GroupPermissionsV2.java:121 — Every restricted user search/count scans all group resources, evaluates authorization for each, and materializes every granted ID without pagination.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() in GroupPermissionsV2.java (lines 108-125) iterates through all group resources using resourceStore.findByType() and evaluates permissions for each one, collecting all granted IDs into a HashSet without any pagination. This is a real performance/scalability concern for realms with many groups. However, this is not a bug per se - it's a design/architecture concern about the new V2 implementation. The code will function correctly but may have performance issues at scale. This is a legitimate non-bug review concern grounded in the actual diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/GroupsResource.java:113 — Removing the global-view short circuit makes paginated group listings run a resource lookup and full authorization evaluation once per returned group.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that in GroupsResource.java, the code changed from `boolean canViewGlobal = groupsEvaluator.canView(); return stream.filter(g -> canViewGlobal || groupsEvaluator.canView(g))` to just `return stream.filter(groupsEvaluator::canView)`. Previously, if canViewGlobal was true, the per-group canView(g) check was short-circuited. Now every group in the stream calls canView(g), which in GroupPermissionsV2 involves hasPermission() calls that do resource lookups and authorization evaluation. This is a legitimate performance concern for paginated listings, though it's a design/architecture issue rather than a bug since the behavior is still correct.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/GroupResource.java:178 — The subgroup endpoint still loads every subgroup before pagination and now performs a full authorization evaluation for each one even when an all-groups permission grants access.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a performance concern in GroupResource.java. The diff shows at line 177-178 that `.filter(auth.groups()::canView)` is applied to every subgroup after loading them all (group.getSubGroupsStream with -1, -1 for no limit), and pagination happens afterward via paginatedStream(). With the new GroupPermissionsV2.canView() implementation, each call potentially performs authorization evaluation including resource lookups and policy evaluation. While this isn't a bug (it's functionally correct), it's a legitimate performance/architecture concern introduced by the change - the authorization check is now potentially more expensive per-call, and the pattern of filtering after loading all items is inefficient.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/GroupPermissionsV2.java:70 — A caller granted only the global Groups view scope passes requireManage() and can create top-level groups.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at GroupPermissionsV2.java lines 63-72, the canManage() method returns true if the user has AdminRoles.MANAGE_USERS OR if hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE) returns true. The hasPermission call with VIEW scope means a user with only VIEW permission on groups would pass canManage(). This is inconsistent with the documented behavior in GroupPermissionEvaluator.java which states canManage() should return true for MANAGE_USERS role or permission to MANAGE groups (not VIEW). The VIEW scope should not grant manage capabilities. This allows users with only view permissions to pass requireManage() checks, potentially enabling unauthorized group creation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/tests/admin/authz/fgap/GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest.java:276 — The all-groups VIEW test never attempts a write, so it misses that canManage() currently accepts VIEW as MANAGE.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the test method testViewGroups() at line 276, it only tests that VIEW permission allows listing groups via groups().groups(). The finding claims the test misses verifying that canManage() incorrectly accepts VIEW scope. Examining GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() in the diff (lines 63-69), it checks for AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW and AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE scopes - meaning VIEW scope would grant manage permission. The test doesn't attempt any write/manage operations after granting VIEW permission, so it wouldn't catch if VIEW incorrectly grants MANAGE access. However, looking more carefully at canManage() method, it uses hasPermission with VIEW and MANAGE scopes, which appears intentional for the 'canManage()' without group parameter (checking if user can manage any groups). The test is specifically for VIEW functionality, not for verifying MANAGE restrictions. This is a valid observation about test coverage gap but the code behavior may be intentional.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/tests/admin/authz/fgap/GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest.java:306 — The membership test only checks that joinGroup returns without an exception and never verifies that Bob actually joined the group.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the test method `testManageGroupMembership()` in the diff, it calls `realmAdminClient.realm(realm.getName()).users().get(bobId).joinGroup(topGroup.getId())` at line 306 but never verifies that Bob actually became a member of the group. The test only checks that the operation doesn't throw an exception. This is a valid test quality concern - the test should verify the actual outcome (e.g., by checking Bob's group memberships). However, this is not a bug in the production code, but rather an incomplete test assertion for newly added test code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/tests/admin/authz/fgap/GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest.java:103 — Coverage exercises only user search, leaving the changed filtered count overloads and brute-force user listing behavior unverified.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows changes to UsersResource.java (lines 395-429) modifying getUsersCount() to use getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() instead of getGroupsWithViewPermission(), and changes to BruteForceUsersResource.java with similar permission logic changes. The new test file GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest.java only tests user search via users().search() but does not test the count endpoints (getUsersCount with various parameters) or the BruteForceUsersResource behavior. These are distinct code paths that were modified but lack test coverage in the new test file.
